drills.q: What percentage of organizations are actively consolidating microservices back into larger units, per the CNCF 2025 report?
True or false: a modular monolith is defined mainly by having a clean folder structure separating concerns.
drills.a: False -- the defining property is ENFORCED, checkable boundaries where a violation is a build/CI failure, not a folder-structure convention that can be silently violated.

drills.q: Name Segment's real-world outcome from over-splitting into 140+ microservices.
drills.a: A shared library change required deploying all 140+ services together, defeating independent deployability -- they consolidated back into a single application.

drills.q: A team wants to split a module into a microservice because 'it feels more scalable.' Is this one of the four defensible justifications? What's missing from the argument?
drills.a: No. It's missing a concrete, evidence-based reason: independent deployment cadence (a real team-blocking conflict), independent scaling profile (a measured, different resource need), fault isolation (a genuinely different, isolatable failure mode), or forced polyglot (a proven language/runtime need). A vague sense that something 'should scale better' is premature optimization without one of these backing it.

drills.q: Explain mechanically why debugging a single user request takes longer in microservices than in a monolith.
drills.a: A monolith's request execution is one call stack in one process, debuggable via a stack trace or log grep. Microservices scatter the same request's execution across multiple processes connected by network calls, requiring distributed tracing with correctly-propagated trace context at every hop -- any hop that fails to propagate context leaves a gap in the trace exactly where the bug likely is.

drills.q: Correctly summarize Amazon Prime Video's 2023 case study, and name the common overstatement of it.
drills.a: One specific monitoring tool was moved from a serverless/microservices design to a monolith, cutting infrastructure cost 90%. Common overstatement: treating this as 'Amazon abandoned microservices for the entire Prime Video platform' -- it was scoped to one tool, starting from a serverless architecture, not a general microservices claim across the platform.

drills.q: Is 'monorepo' synonymous with 'monolith,' and 'polyrepo' synonymous with 'microservices'? Give real counter-examples.
drills.a: No, they're orthogonal decisions. Shopify runs a monorepo housing a modular monolith. Amazon runs polyrepo with real microservices. Google runs a monorepo housing many independently-deployed services -- all valid, real combinations depending on whether cross-cutting refactor ease or per-team deployment autonomy matters more.

drills.q: A team's monolith deploy pipeline takes 45 minutes and Team A is repeatedly blocked by Team B's unrelated changes going through the same release. Is a full microservices decomposition the right response? What's the more targeted alternative?
drills.a: This is a real instance of justification #1 (independent deployment cadence), so SOME split is directionally justified -- but the right move is extracting the specific component(s) causing the actual blocking, not a wholesale fine-grained decomposition. A narrower fix (better feature flagging, decoupling the deploy pipeline for unrelated modules within the same codebase) might resolve the pain without paying the full distributed-systems cost.

drills.q: Design the extraction path for pulling a genuinely justified microservice out of a modular monolith. What's the most common mistake to avoid?
drills.a: 1) Confirm the module already has enforced in-process boundaries -- extracting an unenforced boundary just moves it across a network, making it worse. 2) Resolve data ownership BEFORE extraction, converting any cross-module data access to an API call first. 3) Extract behind a stable interface matching how it was called in-process. 4) Shadow-then-gradual-cutover, monitoring for new latency/partial-failure modes. Most common mistake: extracting the code before resolving data ownership, leaving the new 'service' still reading/writing the monolith's shared database directly -- recreating coupling through the schema while paying full network/deployment overhead.

drills.q: A 30-service microservices fleet is genuinely painful to operate. Should the team consolidate everything back to one monolith? How would you decide which services to consolidate?
drills.a: Not a blanket full consolidation -- diagnose empirically which services are actually causing pain. Check deployment logs for services frequently deployed together (tight coupling, Segment-style consolidation candidates) and check whether each service has ever actually exercised independent scaling or had an isolated failure that mattered (weak justification if never) versus services with a documented instance of either (stronger case to keep separate). Consolidate the evidence-backed coupled/painful subset, not the whole fleet reflexively.
